title: The Debate: Linguistic Imperialism
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A balanced look at one of the most heated debates in modern language study: does the global spread of English empower people, or does it quietly kill off the world's other languages?
competenceGoals: analyze the position of English in the world
reflect on the role of English in international contexts and its impact on other languages and cultures

content.content:
## Does English Threaten Other Languages?

There are roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today. Linguists estimate that by the end of this century, somewhere between half and ninety percent of them will have vanished. Many people point an accusing finger at the global dominance of English. But is that fair? Does learning and using English really have to come at the expense of other languages -- or can English coexist with, and even support, a diverse linguistic world?

These are not just dusty academic questions. They affect real communities, real cultures, and real people -- including Norwegians, who constantly navigate the relationship between their own language and the global reach of English. This chapter looks at both sides of a genuinely contested debate. On one side stands the linguist **Robert Phillipson**, who argues that the spread of English is a form of imperialism. On the other stand critics who insist that English is a neutral tool people freely choose. As you will see, the truth is more complicated than either position alone.

## Phillipson's Case: Linguistic Imperialism

In 1992, the Danish linguist **Robert Phillipson** published a controversial book called *Linguistic Imperialism*. His central claim was bold: the global spread of English is *not* natural or neutral. Instead, it is the result of deliberate policies that serve the interests of English-speaking powers.

Phillipson argued that the UK and USA have actively promoted English worldwide through organisations like the British Council and USAID, advancing their own political and economic interests. As English spreads, he claimed, it does so at the expense of other languages, contributing to their decline and even death. And because native speakers always hold an automatic advantage, the dominance of English builds in a permanent structural inequality. He also challenged five common beliefs about English teaching that he saw as ideology dressed up as fact: that English is best taught only in English; that the ideal teacher is a native speaker; that the earlier English is introduced the better; that more English always means better results; and that other languages get in the way of learning English. None of these, he argued, is a proven truth -- each conveniently serves the English-speaking world and the global English-teaching industry, worth over 60 billion dollars.

The stakes become vivid when you look at **language death**. When the last fluent speaker of Eyak, Marie Smith Jones, died in Alaska in 2008, a unique way of understanding the world disappeared forever. The same happened to Livonian in Latvia in 2013. Of the world's 7,000 languages, around 3,000 are classed as endangered; several Sami varieties in Norway, Sweden, and Finland have fewer than 100 speakers. When a language dies, we lose not just words but oral literature, songs, traditional ecological knowledge, and a community's connection to its own history. In many cases, the shift happens because speakers see greater economic opportunity in a larger language and stop passing on their own.

questions.task: According to Robert Phillipson, the global spread of English is mainly:

options.text: A natural and inevitable result of globalisation
Entirely beneficial for everyone worldwide
The result of deliberate policies serving English-speaking powers
A process that has already stopped

questions.solution: Phillipson argues the spread of English is not natural or neutral but the product of deliberate policies by English-speaking countries and the global English-teaching industry -- a form of cultural imperialism.

options.text: When a language gets a new alphabet
When a language borrows foreign words
When two languages merge into one
When the last native speakers die without passing the language to the next generation

questions.solution: Language death occurs when a language ceases to be spoken because its last native speakers die without transmitting it to children -- as happened with Eyak in 2008.

questions.task: Which belief did Phillipson challenge as ideology rather than fact?

options.text: The idea that the ideal English teacher is a native speaker
The idea that languages can die out
The idea that English has many speakers
The idea that English borrowed from French

questions.solution: Phillipson challenged five tenets of English teaching, including the belief that native speakers are the ideal teachers -- arguing these serve the interests of English-speaking countries rather than being proven facts.

content.content:
## The Other Side: Choice, Ownership, and Complexity

Not everyone accepts Phillipson's view, and the counter-arguments are serious.

First, there is the question of **agency and choice**. People learn English because they see real benefits -- jobs, education, travel -- not because they are forced. Parents actively *want* English education for their children. To frame all English learners as helpless victims of imperialism, critics say, denies them their own decision-making. Second, **English no longer belongs to Britain or the USA**. The whole World Englishes movement shows that people adapt English to their own cultures; Indian English, Nigerian English, and Singlish are creative, not deficient. Third, English can be a **neutral tool**: in multilingual countries, it often serves as a lingua franca that does not favour any single local ethnic group -- in India, English is sometimes preferred over Hindi precisely because Hindi favours the north. Fourth, learning English usually means **multilingualism, not replacement**: Scandinavians speak excellent English while keeping their own languages fully alive. And fifth, **language death has many causes** -- urbanisation, economic pressure, government policy -- and English is not always the culprit; many endangered languages are threatened by other dominant languages like Mandarin, Spanish, or Russian.

So where does this leave us? The debate connects to the broader idea of **language rights** -- the right of communities to use, maintain, and develop their own languages. International frameworks like the Universal Declaration of Linguistic Rights (1996) and the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages (1992) try to protect these rights. Practical approaches aim for balance: **additive multilingualism** (adding English without dropping local languages), **mother-tongue education**, **language documentation** of endangered tongues, **parallel language use** across different domains (as Norway does), and **terminology development** so local languages keep pace with science and technology. As a Norwegian student, you sit in a fascinating position: you gain from English while keeping a strong national language. Understanding this debate helps you think critically about your own relationship with the world's most powerful language.

People freely choose to learn English because of its real benefits

Banning all languages except English

Teaching only one language at a time

questions.task: Why might English be preferred as a 'neutral' language in a multilingual country?

options.text: It is the oldest language in the country
It has no grammar rules
It is spoken by everyone natively
It does not favour any single local ethnic group

questions.solution: In multilingual nations, English can act as a neutral lingua franca because it does not privilege one local group -- in India, for instance, English avoids favouring the Hindi-speaking north.

content.content:
## Summary

The debate over **linguistic imperialism** has no easy answer. **Robert Phillipson** argues that English spreads through deliberate policy serving English-speaking powers, builds in structural inequality, and contributes to **language death** -- a real crisis, given that thousands of the world's 7,000 languages are endangered. His critics counter that people exercise genuine **agency** in choosing English, that English now belongs to everyone through World Englishes, that it can serve as a **neutral** lingua franca, that learning it usually means **multilingualism rather than replacement**, and that language death has many causes beyond English. The way forward lies in protecting **language rights** through approaches like additive multilingualism, mother-tongue education, and parallel language use. As a Norwegian student, you both benefit from English and keep a strong national language -- a position that lets you weigh this debate thoughtfully and responsibly.
